title: Kodak: Inventing the Future It Couldn't Sell
subtitle: A company whose own researcher built a digital camera in 1975, but whose richest margins came from film, paper, chemicals and processing, the sales digital substitution hit hardest.
cardSubtitle: It built a digital camera in 1975; digital never carried film's margins.

keyHighlights.title: Invented at Home
keyHighlights.description: A Kodak researcher built a digital camera prototype in 1975, about the size of a toaster.

keyHighlights.title: Paid on Every Picture
keyHighlights.description: Film, paper, chemicals and processing could earn again each time someone took a photo.

keyHighlights.title: Digital Up, Margin Down
keyHighlights.description: Digital revenue overtook traditional revenue in 2005, while gross margin fell to 25.6%.

content.text: The object above is a photograph of film, propped on a worn wooden counter: one 35mm roll standing in its small metal canister, its leader curling out, with more canisters and coils of film around it. The film in the picture and the paper it is printed on are, between them, a fair portrait of how Eastman Kodak made its money.

content.text: The awkward twist is that the threat was first built inside the company. In 1975 a Kodak researcher built what the company calls the world's first digital camera, a toaster-sized prototype that captured black-and-white images of 10,000 pixels. Kodak did not miss the future; it had a working prototype of it in 1975. The hard part was living with it.

content.text: Kodak's annual report for fiscal 1996 spelled out the model. Amateur photography needed, at minimum, a camera, film and photofinishing, and photofinishing needed chemicals and paper for prints. Kodak supplied all of it.

content.text: The camera opened the door; the pictures paid the rent. Each roll bought, developed and printed was another chance to sell film, paper, chemicals or processing. In fiscal 1996 Kodak reported about $16.0 billion of sales and roughly $7.6 billion of gross profit, close to 48 cents of every sales dollar.

What the digital camera deleted

content.text: A digital camera has no roll to replace: the next picture needs no film, no chemicals and no lab. Kodak's fiscal 2003 annual report named the damage. Digital substitution had hit mainly its film and paper sales and processing services in the U.S., Japan and Western Europe, and it expected U.S. consumer film industry volumes to fall 10% to 12% in 2004.

content.text: Before asking whether an incumbent can build the new product, ask what the new product deletes. When it deletes the repeat purchase that pays for everything else, the company must replace its income, not just its product line.

sections.title: Winning the Sales, Losing the Margin

content.text: Kodak did go digital, and seriously. It introduced a professional digital camera system in 1991, launched EasyShare consumer cameras in 2001 and, by its own count, shipped its 100 millionth digital still camera in 2011. Its 2003 strategy combined managing the traditional business for cash with faster digital growth, among other goals.

content.text: By fiscal 2005 digital revenues, swelled by acquired printing businesses, had overtaken traditional ones. The trouble was the kind of revenue it was. On about $14.3 billion of sales, gross margin slipped to 25.6% from 29.1% a year earlier, and the annual report named consumer digital cameras first in explaining the price and mix declines. Its fiscal 2003 report had already warned that rapid price declines soon after a model's launch were common.

content.text: This is a value trap of strategy: a business too profitable to abandon. The further Kodak's sales shifted from film toward lower-margin digital products, led by cameras under steady price pressure, the thinner its margin became.

content.text: The reckoning came in 2012. Kodak filed for Chapter 11 in January, said in February it would exit its business of digital cameras, pocket video cameras and digital picture frames, and in December agreed to sell and license its digital imaging patents in deals worth about $525 million. It emerged in September 2013, completing that day the spin-off of its personalized imaging and document imaging businesses to the pension plan of its U.K. subsidiary.

content.text: The telling detail is in printing. A new plate is needed for every print run, which the filing calls a recurring revenue stream, and the plate-making business supplied about half of fiscal 2025 revenue. Kodak rebuilt itself around a consumable again, sold to printers instead of households.

content.text: Two honest limits. The 1996 and 2005 margins describe different companies, since Kodak sold and bought whole businesses in between, and its 2005 cost of goods sold carried about $430 million of restructuring charges, so the comparison shows direction, not precision. And hindsight flatters the critic: the filings show how hard it was to give up a meter that ran on every picture, not what a film company should have become.
